chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter II
paragraphs: On the twenty-ninth of May Napoleon left Dresden, where he had spent three weeks surrounded by a court that included princes, dukes, kings, and even an emperor. Before leaving, Napoleon showed favor to the emperor, kings, and princes who had earned it, scolded the kings and princes he was displeased with, presented pearls and diamonds of his own — that is, those he had taken from other kings — to the Empress of Austria, and having, as his historian tells us, tenderly embraced the Empress Marie Louise — who regarded him as her husband, though he had left another wife in Paris — left her grieved by the parting which she seemed hardly able to bear. Though the diplomats still firmly believed in the possibility of peace and worked hard to that end, and though Emperor Napoleon himself wrote a letter to Alexander calling him Monsieur mon frere and sincerely assuring him that he did not want war and would always love and honor him — yet he set off to join his army, and at every station gave fresh orders to speed up the movement of his troops from west to east. He traveled in a coach with six horses, surrounded by pages, aides-de-camp, and an escort, along the road to Posen, Thorn, Danzig, and Konigsberg. At each of these towns thousands of people met him with excitement and enthusiasm.

The army was moving from west to east, and relays of six horses carried him in the same direction. On June tenth, coming up with the army, he spent the night in quarters prepared for him on the estate of a Polish count in the Vilkavisski forest.
(Old style date.)
Next day, overtaking the army, he went in a carriage to the Niemen, and changing into a Polish uniform, drove to the riverbank to select a place for the crossing.

Seeing on the other side some Cossacks and the wide-spreading steppes in the midst of which lay the holy city of Moscow, the capital of a realm such as the Scythia into which Alexander the Great had marched — Napoleon unexpectedly, and contrary alike to strategic and diplomatic considerations, ordered an advance, and the next day his army began to cross the Niemen.

Early in the morning of June twelfth, he came out of his tent, which was pitched that day on the steep left bank of the Niemen, and looked through a spyglass at the streams of his troops pouring out of the Vilkavisski forest and flowing over the three bridges thrown across the river. The troops, knowing of the Emperor's presence, were on the lookout for him, and when they caught sight of a figure in an overcoat and a cocked hat standing apart from his suite in front of his tent on the hill, they threw up their caps and shouted: "Vive l'Empereur!" and one after another poured in a ceaseless stream out of the vast forest that had concealed them and, splitting apart, flowed on and on across the three bridges to the other side.

"Now we'll get into action. Oh, when he takes it in hand himself, things get hot... by heaven!... There he is!... Vive l'Empereur! So these are the steppes of Asia! It's a miserable country all the same. Goodbye, Beauche — I'll save the best palace in Moscow for you! Goodbye. Good luck!... Did you see the Emperor? Vive l'Empereur!... If they make me Governor of India, Gerard, I'll make you Minister of Kashmir — that's settled. Vive l'Empereur! Hurrah! hurrah! hurrah! The Cossacks — those rascals — see how they run! Vive l'Empereur! There he is, do you see him? I've seen him twice, as I see you now. The little corporal... I saw him give the cross to one of the veterans... Vive l'Empereur!" came the voices of men, old and young, of the most diverse characters and social positions. On the faces of all was one common expression of joy at the start of the long-expected campaign and of adoration and devotion to the man in the gray coat who was standing on the hill.

On June thirteenth, a rather small, thoroughbred Arab horse was brought to Napoleon. He mounted it and rode at a gallop to one of the bridges over the Niemen, deafened by constant rapturous cheering which he clearly endured only because it was impossible to forbid the soldiers from expressing their love for him this way, but which disturbed him and distracted him from the military concerns that had occupied him from the moment he joined the army. He rode across one of the swaying pontoon bridges to the other side, turned sharply to the left, and galloped toward Kovno, preceded by mounted chasseurs of the Guard who, breathless with delight, galloped ahead to clear a path for him through the troops. On reaching the broad river Viliya, he stopped near a regiment of Polish Uhlans stationed by the river.
"Vivat!" shouted the Poles ecstatically, breaking their ranks and pressing against one another to see him.

Napoleon looked up and down the river, dismounted, and sat down on a log lying on the bank. At a silent signal from him, a telescope was handed to him, which he rested on the back of a happy page who had run up, and he gazed at the opposite bank. Then he became absorbed in a map laid out on the logs. Without lifting his head, he said something, and two of his aides-de-camp galloped off to the Polish Uhlans.
"What? What did he say?" was heard in the ranks of the Polish Uhlans when one of the aides-de-camp rode up to them.

The order was to find a ford and cross the river. The colonel of the Polish Uhlans, a handsome old man, flushed and stammering with excitement, asked the aide-de-camp whether he would be permitted to swim the river with his Uhlans instead of looking for a ford. In obvious fear of refusal, like a boy asking permission to ride a horse, he begged to be allowed to swim across before the Emperor's eyes. The aide-de-camp replied that probably the Emperor would not be displeased by this excess of zeal.

As soon as the aide-de-camp said this, the old mustachioed officer, his face glowing with happiness and his eyes sparkling, raised his saber, shouted "Vivat!" and commanding the Uhlans to follow him, spurred his horse and galloped into the river. He gave an angry kick to his horse, which had grown restive, and plunged into the water, heading for the deepest part where the current was swift. Hundreds of Uhlans galloped in after him. It was cold and frightening in the swift current in the middle of the stream, and the Uhlans grabbed at one another as they fell off their horses. Some of the horses drowned and some of the men; the others tried to swim on, some in the saddle and some clinging to their horses' manes. They tried to reach the opposite bank and, though there was a ford a third of a mile away, were proud that they were swimming and drowning in this river under the eyes of the man who sat on the log and wasn't even looking at what they were doing. When the aide-de-camp, having returned and choosing an opportune moment, dared to draw the Emperor's attention to the devotion of the Poles to his person, the little man in the gray overcoat got up and, having summoned Berthier, began pacing up and down the bank with him, giving him instructions and occasionally glancing disapprovingly at the drowning Uhlans who were distracting his attention.

For him it was no new conviction that his presence in any part of the world, from Africa to the steppes of Russia alike, was enough to overwhelm people and drive them to insane self-sacrifice. He called for his horse and rode to his quarters.

Some forty Uhlans drowned in the river, though boats were sent to help them. The majority struggled back to the bank from which they had started. The colonel and some of his men got across and with difficulty scrambled out on the far bank. And as soon as they had gotten out, in their soaked and streaming clothes, they shouted "Vivat!" and gazed ecstatically at the spot where Napoleon had been but where he no longer was — and at that moment considered themselves happy.

That evening, between issuing one order that the counterfeit Russian paper money prepared for use in Russia should be delivered as quickly as possible and another that a Saxon should be shot on whom a letter had been found containing information about French army orders, Napoleon also gave instructions that the Polish colonel who had needlessly plunged into the river should be enrolled in the Legion of Honor, of which Napoleon was himself the head.
Quos vult perdere dementat.
("Those whom God wishes to destroy, He first drives mad.")

chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter III
paragraphs: The Emperor of Russia had meanwhile been in Vilna for more than a month, reviewing troops and holding maneuvers. Nothing was ready for the war that everyone expected and to prepare for which the Emperor had come from Petersburg. There was no general plan of action. The uncertainty about the various plans that had been proposed had only increased after the Emperor had spent a month at headquarters. Each of the three armies had its own commander in chief, but there was no supreme commander of all the forces, and the Emperor did not take on that responsibility himself.

The longer the Emperor stayed in Vilna, the less did everyone — tired of waiting — prepare for the war. All the efforts of those surrounding the sovereign seemed aimed merely at making him spend his time pleasantly and forget that war was looming.

In June, after many balls and celebrations given by the Polish magnates, by the courtiers, and by the Emperor himself, it occurred to one of the Polish aides-de-camp in attendance that a dinner and ball should be given for the Emperor by his aides-de-camp. This idea was eagerly received. The Emperor gave his consent. The aides-de-camp collected money by subscription. The lady thought most likely to please the Emperor was invited to act as hostess. Count Bennigsen, being a landowner in the Vilna province, offered his country house for the occasion, and June thirteenth was fixed for a ball, dinner, boat race, and fireworks at Zakret, Count Bennigsen's country estate.

The very day that Napoleon issued the order to cross the Niemen, and his vanguard drove off the Cossacks and crossed the Russian frontier, Alexander spent the evening at the party given by his aides-de-camp at Bennigsen's country house.

It was a gay and brilliant celebration. Connoisseurs declared that rarely had so many beautiful women been assembled in one place. Countess Bezukhova was present among other Russian ladies who had followed the sovereign from Petersburg to Vilna, and outshone the refined Polish ladies with her impressive, typically Russian beauty. The Emperor noticed her and honored her with a dance.

Boris Drubetskoy, having left his wife in Moscow and being for the time being a bachelor (as he put it), was also there and, though not an aide-de-camp, had contributed a large sum toward the expenses. Boris was now a rich man who had risen to high rank and no longer sought patronage but stood on equal footing with the most prominent men of his own age. He was meeting Helene in Vilna after not having seen her for a long time and did not dwell on the past, but as Helene was enjoying the favors of a very important personage and Boris had only recently married, they met as good old friends.

At midnight the dancing was still going on. Helene, not having a suitable partner, offered to dance the mazurka with Boris. They were the third couple. Boris, coolly looking at Helene's dazzling bare shoulders which emerged from a dark, gold-embroidered gauze gown, talked to her of old acquaintances and at the same time — unaware of it himself and unnoticed by others — never for an instant stopped watching the Emperor, who was in the same room. The Emperor was not dancing; he stood in the doorway, stopping now one couple and now another with gracious words that he alone knew how to deliver.

As the mazurka began, Boris saw that Adjutant General Balashev, one of those closest to the Emperor, went up to him and — contrary to court etiquette — stood near him while he was talking to a Polish lady. Having finished speaking to her, the Emperor looked inquiringly at Balashev and, evidently understanding that he acted this way only because there were important reasons for doing so, gave a slight nod to the lady and turned to Balashev. Hardly had Balashev begun to speak before a look of amazement appeared on the Emperor's face. He took Balashev by the arm and crossed the room with him, unconsciously clearing a path seven yards wide as people on both sides made way for him. Boris noticed Arakcheev's agitated face when the sovereign left with Balashev. Arakcheev looked at the Emperor from under his brow and, sniffing with his red nose, stepped forward from the crowd as if expecting the Emperor to address him. (Boris understood that Arakcheev envied Balashev and was displeased that evidently important news had reached the Emperor through someone other than himself.)
But the Emperor and Balashev passed out into the illuminated garden without noticing Arakcheev, who, holding his sword and glancing angrily around, followed about twenty paces behind them.

All the time Boris was going through the figures of the mazurka, he was preoccupied with the question of what news Balashev had brought and how he could find it out before others. In the figure where he had to choose two ladies, he whispered to Helene that he meant to choose Countess Potocka who, he thought, had gone out onto the veranda, and glided across the parquet toward the door opening into the garden, where, seeing Balashev and the Emperor returning to the veranda, he stopped. They were moving toward the door. Boris, fluttering as if he hadn't had time to withdraw, respectfully pressed close to the doorpost with bowed head.
The Emperor, with the agitation of a man who has been personally offended, was finishing with these words:

"To enter Russia without declaring war! I will not make peace as long as a single armed enemy remains on my soil!" It seemed to Boris that it gave the Emperor pleasure to utter these words. He was satisfied with the way he had expressed his thoughts but displeased that Boris had overheard them.
"Let no one know of it!" the Emperor added with a frown.
Boris understood that this was meant for him and, closing his eyes, slightly bowed his head. The Emperor re-entered the ballroom and stayed about another half hour.

Boris was thus the first to learn that the French army had crossed the Niemen, and thanks to this was able to show certain important personages that much that was hidden from others was usually known to him, and by this means he rose higher in their estimation.

The unexpected news of the French having crossed the Niemen was particularly startling after a month of unfulfilled expectations, and at a ball. On first receiving the news, under the influence of outrage and resentment, the Emperor had found a phrase that pleased him, fully expressed his feelings, and has since become famous. On returning home at two o'clock that night he sent for his secretary, Shishkov, and told him to write an order to the troops and a rescript to Field Marshal Prince Saltykov, in which he insisted on the words being included that he would not make peace so long as a single armed Frenchman remained on Russian soil.
The next day the following letter was sent to Napoleon:
Monsieur mon frere,

Yesterday I learned that, despite the loyalty with which I have kept my commitments to Your Majesty, your troops have crossed the Russian frontier, and I have this moment received from Petersburg a note in which Count Lauriston states, as a reason for this aggression, that Your Majesty has considered yourself to be in a state of war with me from the time Prince Kurakin asked for his passports. The reasons on which the Duc de Bassano based his refusal to deliver them to him would never have led me to suppose that could serve as a pretext for aggression. In fact, the ambassador, as he himself has declared, was never authorized to make that demand, and as soon as I was informed of it I let him know how much I disapproved of it and ordered him to remain at his post. If Your Majesty does not intend to shed the blood of our peoples for such a misunderstanding, and consents to withdraw your troops from Russian territory, I will regard what has passed as not having occurred and an understanding between us will be possible. In the contrary case, Your Majesty, I shall see myself forced to repel an attack that nothing on my part has provoked. It still depends on Your Majesty to preserve humanity from the calamity of another war.
I am, etc.,
(signed) Alexander

chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter IV
paragraphs: At two in the morning of June fourteenth, the Emperor, having sent for Balashev and read him his letter to Napoleon, ordered him to take it and deliver it personally to the French Emperor. When dispatching Balashev, the Emperor repeated his words about not making peace so long as a single armed enemy remained on Russian soil, and told him to convey those words to Napoleon. Alexander did not include them in his letter to Napoleon because, with his characteristic tact, he felt it would be inappropriate to use them at a moment when a last attempt at reconciliation was being made; but he specifically instructed Balashev to repeat them personally to Napoleon.

Having set off in the early hours of the fourteenth, accompanied by a bugler and two Cossacks, Balashev reached the French outposts at the village of Rykonty, on the Russian side of the Niemen, by dawn. There he was stopped by French cavalry sentinels.

A French noncommissioned officer of hussars, in a crimson uniform and a shaggy cap, shouted to the approaching Balashev to halt. Balashev did not do so immediately, but continued to advance along the road at a walking pace.

The noncommissioned officer frowned and, muttering curses, rode his horse's chest against Balashev, put his hand on his saber, and shouted rudely at the Russian general, asking: was he deaf that he did not obey orders? Balashev gave his name. The noncommissioned officer began talking with his comrades about regimental matters without looking at the Russian general.

After living at the center of the highest authority and power, after conversing with the Emperor less than three hours before, and being generally accustomed to the respect due to his rank, Balashev found it very strange here on Russian soil to encounter this hostile, and still more this disrespectful, use of brute force against himself.

The sun was just appearing from behind the clouds, the air was fresh and dewy. A herd of cattle was being driven along the road from the village, and over the fields larks rose trilling, one after another, like bubbles rising in water.
Balashev looked around him, awaiting the arrival of an officer from the village. The Russian Cossacks and bugler and the French hussars looked silently at one another from time to time.

A French colonel of hussars, who had obviously just left his bed, came riding from the village on a handsome sleek gray horse, accompanied by two hussars. The officer, the soldiers, and their horses all looked smart and well-groomed.

It was that early stage of a campaign when troops are still in full trim, almost like peacetime maneuvers, but with a touch of martial swagger in their clothing and a hint of the gaiety and adventurous spirit that always accompany the opening of a campaign.

The French colonel, struggling to suppress a yawn, was polite and clearly understood Balashev's importance. He led him past his soldiers and behind the outposts and said that his wish to be presented to the Emperor would most likely be granted immediately, as the Emperor's quarters were believed to be not far off.

They rode through the village of Rykonty, past tethered French hussar horses, past sentinels and men who saluted their colonel and stared with curiosity at the Russian uniform, and came out at the other end of the village. The colonel said that the division commander was a mile and a quarter away and would receive Balashev and conduct him to his destination.
The sun had by now risen and shone gaily on the bright green landscape.

They had hardly ridden up a hill, past a tavern, before they saw a group of horsemen coming toward them. In front of the group, on a black horse with trappings that glittered in the sun, rode a tall man with plumes in his hat and black hair curling down to his shoulders. He wore a red cloak, and stretched his long legs forward in French fashion. This man rode toward Balashev at a gallop, his plumes streaming and his gems and gold lace glittering in the bright June sunshine.

Balashev was only two horses' lengths from the rider with the bracelets, plumes, necklaces, and gold embroidery, who was galloping toward him with a theatrically solemn expression, when the French colonel Julner whispered respectfully: "The King of Naples!" It was in fact Murat, now called "King of Naples." Though it was quite incomprehensible why he should be King of Naples, he was called so, and was himself convinced that he was, and therefore assumed a more solemn and important air than before. He was so sure that he really was the King of Naples that when, on the eve of his departure from that city, while walking through the streets with his wife, some Italians called out to him: "Long live the king!" he turned to his wife with a thoughtful smile and said: "Poor fellows, they don't know that I'm leaving them tomorrow!"
(The Italian means: "Long live the king.")

But though he firmly believed himself to be King of Naples and pitied the grief of the subjects he was abandoning, recently, after he had been ordered back to military service — and especially since his last meeting with Napoleon in Danzig, when his august brother-in-law had told him: "I made you King that you should reign in my way, but not in yours!" — he had cheerfully taken up his familiar business, and like a well-fed but not overfed horse that feels itself in harness and grows frisky between the shafts, he dressed up in the most colorful and expensive clothes possible and galloped gaily and contentedly along the roads of Poland, without himself knowing why or where.

On seeing the Russian general, he threw back his head with its long hair curling to his shoulders in a majestically royal manner, and looked inquiringly at the French colonel. The colonel respectfully informed His Majesty of Balashev's mission, though he couldn't pronounce the name.
"De Bal-macheve!" said the King (overcoming by sheer confidence the difficulty that had stumped the colonel). "Charmed to meet you, General!" he added with a gesture of kingly graciousness.

As soon as the King began to speak loudly and rapidly, his royal dignity instantly deserted him, and without noticing it he slipped into his natural tone of good-natured familiarity. He laid his hand on the withers of Balashev's horse and said:
"Well, General, it all looks like war," as if regretting a circumstance he was powerless to judge.

"Your Majesty," replied Balashev, "my master, the Emperor, does not desire war, and as Your Majesty sees..." said Balashev, using the words "Your Majesty" at every opportunity, with the deliberateness unavoidable when frequently addressing someone to whom the title was still a novelty.

Murat's face beamed with foolish satisfaction as he listened to "Monsieur de Bal-macheve." But royalty has its obligations! And he felt it incumbent on him, as a king and an ally, to discuss state affairs with Alexander's envoy. He dismounted, took Balashev's arm, and moving a few steps away from his suite, which waited respectfully, began to walk up and down with him, trying to speak meaningfully. He mentioned that the Emperor Napoleon had been offended by the demand that he withdraw his troops from Prussia, especially when that demand became publicly known and the dignity of France was thereby insulted.
(The French phrase means: "Royalty has its obligations.")
Balashev replied that there was "nothing offensive in the demand, because..." but Murat interrupted him.
"Then you don't consider the Emperor Alexander the aggressor?" he asked unexpectedly, with a kindly and foolish smile.
Balashev told him why he considered Napoleon to be the instigator of the war.

"Oh, my dear general!" Murat interrupted again, "with all my heart I wish the Emperors may settle this between themselves, and that the war — begun through no wish of mine — may end as quickly as possible!" said he, in the tone of a servant who wants to stay on good terms with another servant despite a quarrel between their masters.

And he went on to ask about the Grand Duke and the state of his health, and to reminisce about the gay and amusing times he had spent with him in Naples. Then suddenly, as if remembering his royal dignity, Murat solemnly drew himself up, assumed the pose he had struck at his coronation, and waving his right arm, said:

"I won't detain you longer, General. I wish success to your mission," and with his embroidered red cloak, his flowing plumes, and his glittering ornaments, he rejoined his suite, who were respectfully waiting.

Balashev rode on, expecting from Murat's words that he would very soon be brought before Napoleon himself. But instead, at the next village, sentinels of Davout's infantry corps detained him just as the vanguard pickets had done, and an adjutant of the corps commander was sent for and conducted him to the village to Marshal Davout.

chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter V
paragraphs: Davout was to Napoleon what Arakcheev was to Alexander — though not a coward like Arakcheev, he was equally precise, equally cruel, and equally unable to express his devotion to his sovereign except through cruelty.

In the organism of states such men are necessary, as wolves are necessary in the organism of nature, and they always exist, always appear and hold their ground, however incongruous their presence and proximity to the head of government may be. This inevitability alone can explain how the cruel Arakcheev, who tore out a grenadier's mustache with his own hands, whose weak nerves made him unable to face danger, and who was neither an educated man nor a courtier, was able to maintain his powerful position with Alexander, whose own character was chivalrous, noble, and gentle.

Balashev found Davout seated on a barrel in the shed of a peasant's hut, writing — he was auditing accounts. Better quarters could have been found for him, but Marshal Davout was one of those men who purposely put themselves in the most uncomfortable conditions to justify their being gloomy. For the same reason they are always hard at work and in a hurry. "How can I think about the bright side of life when, as you see, I'm sitting on a barrel and working in a dirty shed?" the expression on his face seemed to say. The chief pleasure and need of such men, when they encounter anyone who shows energy, is to display their own dreary, relentless activity. Davout indulged this pleasure when Balashev was brought in. He became still more absorbed in his work when the Russian general entered, and after glancing over his spectacles at Balashev's face — which was animated by the beauty of the morning and by his conversation with Murat — he did not rise or even stir, but scowled more deeply and sneered maliciously.
When he noticed the unpleasant impression this reception made on Balashev's face, Davout raised his head and coldly asked what he wanted.

Thinking he could only have been received this way because Davout didn't know that he was adjutant general to Emperor Alexander and even his envoy to Napoleon, Balashev hastened to state his rank and mission. Contrary to his expectation, Davout, after hearing him, became still surlier and ruder.
"Where is your dispatch?" he demanded. "Give it to me. I will send it to the Emperor."
Balashev replied that he had been ordered to hand it personally to the Emperor.
"Your Emperor's orders are obeyed in your army, but here," said Davout, "you must do as you're told."
And, as if to make the Russian general still more conscious of his helplessness before brute force, Davout sent an adjutant to call the officer on duty.

Balashev took out the packet containing the Emperor's letter and laid it on the table (made of a door with its hinges still attached, laid across two barrels). Davout took the packet and read the inscription.
"You are perfectly free to treat me with respect or not," protested Balashev, "but permit me to point out that I have the honor of being adjutant general to His Majesty..."
Davout glanced at him silently and clearly took pleasure in the signs of agitation and confusion on Balashev's face.
"You will be treated as is fitting," said he and, putting the packet in his pocket, left the shed.
A minute later the marshal's adjutant, de Castres, came in and took Balashev to the quarters assigned to him.
That day he dined with the marshal, at the same board on the barrels.

The next day Davout rode out early and, after calling for Balashev, bluntly ordered him to remain where he was, to move on with the baggage train if orders came for it to move, and to speak to no one except Monsieur de Castres.

After four days of solitude, boredom, and a painful sense of his own powerlessness and insignificance — particularly acute by contrast with the sphere of power in which he had so recently moved — and after several marches with the marshal's baggage and the French army, which occupied the whole district, Balashev was brought to Vilna — now occupied by the French — through the very gate by which he had left it four days earlier.
The next day the imperial gentleman-in-waiting, the Count de Turenne, came to Balashev and informed him of Emperor Napoleon's wish to honor him with an audience.

Four days before, sentinels of the Preobrazhensky regiment had stood in front of the house to which Balashev was conducted, and now two French grenadiers stood there in blue uniforms unbuttoned in front with shaggy caps on their heads, and an escort of hussars and Uhlans and a brilliant suite of aides-de-camp, pages, and generals, waiting for Napoleon to come out, were standing at the porch around his saddle horse and his Mameluke, Rustan. Napoleon received Balashev in the very house in Vilna from which Alexander had dispatched him on his mission.

chapters.title: Book Nine (1812) — Chapter VI
paragraphs: Though Balashev was accustomed to imperial magnificence, he was amazed at the luxury and splendor of Napoleon's court.

The Count de Turenne showed him into a large reception room where many generals, gentlemen-in-waiting, and Polish magnates — several of whom Balashev had seen at the court of the Emperor of Russia — were waiting. Duroc said that Napoleon would receive the Russian general before going for his ride.
After some minutes, the gentleman-in-waiting on duty came into the great reception room and, bowing politely, asked Balashev to follow him.

Balashev went into a small reception room, one door of which led into a study — the very one from which the Russian Emperor had dispatched him on his mission. He stood a minute or two, waiting. He heard hurried footsteps beyond the door, both halves of it were opened rapidly; all was silent, and then from the study came the sound of other steps, firm and resolute — those of Napoleon. He had just finished dressing for his ride and wore a blue uniform, opening in front over a white waistcoat so long that it covered his round stomach, white leather breeches tightly fitting the plump thighs of his short legs, and Hessian boots. His short hair had obviously just been brushed, but one lock hung down in the middle of his broad forehead. His plump white neck stood out sharply above the black collar of his uniform, and he smelled of cologne. His full face, rather young-looking, with its prominent chin, wore a gracious and majestic expression of imperial welcome.

He entered briskly, with a bounce at every step and his head slightly thrown back. His whole short, stout figure, with its broad thick shoulders and chest and stomach naturally jutting forward, had that imposing and stately appearance one sees in well-fed men of forty. It was also evident that he was in the best of spirits that day.

He nodded in answer to Balashev's low and respectful bow, and coming up to him at once began speaking like a man who values every moment of his time and does not bother preparing what he has to say, confident that he will always say the right thing and say it well.

"Good day, General!" said he. "I have received the letter you brought from the Emperor Alexander and am very glad to see you." He glanced with his large eyes into Balashev's face and immediately looked past him.

It was plain that Balashev's personality did not interest him at all. Clearly only what took place within his own mind interested him. Nothing outside himself had any significance for him, because everything in the world, it seemed to him, depended entirely on his will.
"I do not, and did not, desire war," he continued, "but it has been forced on me. Even now" (he stressed the word) "I am ready to receive any explanations you can give me."

And he began clearly and concisely to explain his reasons for dissatisfaction with the Russian government. Judging by the calmly moderate and friendly tone in which the French Emperor spoke, Balashev was firmly convinced that he wished for peace and intended to enter into negotiations.

When Napoleon, having finished speaking, looked inquiringly at the Russian envoy, Balashev began a speech he had long prepared: "Sire! The Emperor, my master..." but the sight of the Emperor's eyes fixed on him confused him. "You are flustered — compose yourself!" Napoleon seemed to say, as with a barely perceptible smile he looked at Balashev's uniform and sword.

Balashev recovered himself and began to speak. He said that the Emperor Alexander did not consider Kurakin's demand for his passports a sufficient cause for war; that Kurakin had acted on his own initiative and without his sovereign's consent; that the Emperor Alexander did not desire war and had no dealings with England.
"Not yet!" interjected Napoleon, and as if afraid of giving vent to his feelings, he frowned and nodded slightly as a sign that Balashev might continue.

After saying all he had been instructed to say, Balashev added that the Emperor Alexander wished for peace but would not enter into negotiations except on condition that... Here Balashev hesitated: he remembered the words the Emperor Alexander had not written in his letter but had specially inserted in the instructions to Saltykov and had told Balashev to repeat to Napoleon. Balashev remembered these words — "So long as a single armed foe remains on Russian soil" — but some complex feeling held him back. He could not utter them, though he wished to. He grew confused and said: "On condition that the French army retreats beyond the Niemen."

Napoleon noticed Balashev's embarrassment when uttering these last words; his face twitched and the calf of his left leg began to quiver rhythmically. Without moving from where he stood, he began speaking in a louder tone and more hurriedly than before. During the speech that followed, Balashev, who more than once lowered his eyes, involuntarily noticed the quivering of Napoleon's left leg, which increased the more Napoleon raised his voice.

"I desire peace no less than the Emperor Alexander," he began. "Have I not for eighteen months been doing everything to obtain it? I have waited eighteen months for explanations. But to begin negotiations, what is demanded of me?" he said, frowning and making an energetic questioning gesture with his small, white, plump hand.
"The withdrawal of your army beyond the Niemen, sire," replied Balashev.
"The Niemen?" repeated Napoleon. "So now you want me to retreat beyond the Niemen — only the Niemen?" repeated Napoleon, looking straight at Balashev.
Balashev bowed his head respectfully.
Instead of the demand of four months earlier to withdraw from Pomerania, only a withdrawal beyond the Niemen was now demanded. Napoleon turned quickly and began to pace the room.

"You say the demand now is that I should withdraw beyond the Niemen before beginning negotiations, but in exactly the same way two months ago the demand was that I should withdraw beyond the Vistula and the Oder, and yet you are willing to negotiate."

He walked in silence from one corner of the room to the other and again stopped in front of Balashev. Balashev noticed that his left leg was quivering faster than before and his face seemed frozen in its stern expression. This quivering of his left leg was something Napoleon was aware of. "The vibration of my left calf is a great sign with me," he remarked at a later date.

"Such demands as to retreat beyond the Vistula and Oder may be made to a Prince of Baden, but not to me!" Napoleon almost screamed, quite to his own surprise. "If you gave me Petersburg and Moscow I could not accept such conditions. You say I started this war! But who first assembled his army? The Emperor Alexander, not I! And you offer me negotiations when I have spent millions, when you are in alliance with England, and when your position is a bad one. You offer me negotiations! But what is the point of your alliance with England? What has she given you?" he continued hurriedly, clearly no longer trying to show the advantages of peace and discuss its possibility, but only to prove his own rightness and power and Alexander's errors and duplicity.

The beginning of his speech had obviously been intended to demonstrate the advantages of his position and show that he was nevertheless willing to negotiate. But he had started talking, and the more he talked, the less he could control his words.
The whole point of his remarks now was clearly to glorify himself and insult Alexander — exactly what he had least wanted at the start of the conversation.
"I hear you have made peace with Turkey?"
Balashev bowed his head in the affirmative.
"Peace has been concluded..." he began.
But Napoleon did not let him speak. He clearly wanted to do all the talking himself, and continued with the sort of eloquence and uncontrolled irritability to which spoiled people are prone.

"Yes, I know you have made peace with the Turks without getting Moldavia and Wallachia; I would have given your sovereign those provinces, just as I gave him Finland. Yes," he went on, "I promised and would have given the Emperor Alexander Moldavia and Wallachia, and now he won't have those splendid provinces. Yet he might have united them with his empire and in a single reign would have extended Russia from the Gulf of Bothnia to the mouths of the Danube. Catherine the Great could not have done more," said Napoleon, growing more and more excited as he paced up and down the room, repeating to Balashev almost the very words he had used to Alexander himself at Tilsit. "All that, he would have owed to my friendship. Oh, what a splendid reign!" he repeated several times, then paused, drew from his pocket a gold snuffbox, lifted it to his nose, and sniffed at it greedily.
"What a splendid reign the Emperor Alexander's might have been!"
He looked compassionately at Balashev, and as soon as the latter tried to speak, hastily interrupted him.

"What could he wish for or seek that he would not have obtained through my friendship?" demanded Napoleon, shrugging his shoulders in bewilderment. "But no, he has preferred to surround himself with my enemies — and with whom? With Steins, Armfeldts, Bennigsens, and Wintzingerodes! Stein, a traitor expelled from his own country; Armfeldt, a schemer and a rake; Wintzingerode, a fugitive French subject; Bennigsen, somewhat more of a soldier than the others, but still incompetent — a man who was unable to accomplish anything in 1807 and who should awaken terrible memories in the Emperor Alexander's mind... Granted that if they were competent they might be put to use," continued Napoleon — hardly able to keep pace in words with the rush of thoughts that constantly sprang up, proving how right and strong he was (in his mind the two were one and the same) — "but they are not even that! They are fit neither for war nor for peace! Barclay is said to be the most capable of them all, but I can't say so judging by his first moves. And what are they doing, all these courtiers? Pfuel proposes, Armfeldt argues, Bennigsen deliberates, and Barclay, called on to act, doesn't know what to decide, and time passes with nothing done. Bagration alone is a real soldier. He's stupid, but he has experience, a quick eye, and decisiveness... And what role is your young monarch playing in that ridiculous crowd? They compromise him and put the blame for everything on his shoulders. A sovereign should not be with the army unless he is a general!" said Napoleon, clearly aiming these words directly at the Emperor. He knew how much Alexander wanted to be a military commander.
"The campaign started only a week ago, and you haven't even been able to defend Vilna. You are cut in two and have been driven out of the Polish provinces. Your army is grumbling."
"On the contrary, Your Majesty," said Balashev, barely able to remember what had been said to him and struggling to follow these verbal fireworks, "the troops are burning with eagerness..."

"I know everything!" Napoleon interrupted. "I know everything. I know the number of your battalions as exactly as I know my own. You have not two hundred thousand men, and I have three times that number. I give you my word of honor," said Napoleon, forgetting that his word of honor could carry no weight — "I give you my word of honor that I have five hundred and thirty thousand men this side of the Vistula. The Turks will be of no use to you; they are worthless and have shown it by making peace with you. As for the Swedes — it is their fate to be governed by mad kings. Their king was insane and they replaced him with another — Bernadotte, who promptly went mad — for no Swede would ally himself with Russia unless he were mad."
Napoleon grinned maliciously and again raised his snuffbox to his nose.

Balashev knew how to reply to each of Napoleon's remarks and would have done so; he continually made the gesture of a man wishing to say something, but Napoleon always interrupted him. To the alleged insanity of the Swedes, Balashev wanted to reply that when Russia is on her side Sweden is practically an island — but Napoleon gave an angry exclamation to drown his voice. Napoleon was in that state of irritability where a man has to talk, talk, and talk, merely to convince himself that he is in the right. Balashev began to feel uncomfortable: as an envoy he feared to compromise his dignity and felt the need to reply; but as a man he shrank before the torrent of groundless fury that had clearly seized Napoleon. He knew that none of the words now uttered by Napoleon had any significance, and that Napoleon himself would be ashamed of them when he came to his senses. Balashev stood with downcast eyes, watching Napoleon's stout legs pace back and forth and trying to avoid meeting his eyes.
"But what do I care about your allies?" said Napoleon. "I have allies — the Poles. There are eighty thousand of them and they fight like lions. And there will be two hundred thousand of them."

And probably still more agitated by the fact that he had uttered this obvious lie, and that Balashev still stood silently before him in the same attitude of submission to fate, Napoleon abruptly turned around, drew close to Balashev's face, and gesticulating rapidly and energetically with his white hands, almost shouted:

"Know that if you stir up Prussia against me, I'll wipe it off the map of Europe!" he declared, his face pale and distorted by anger, and he struck one small hand energetically against the other. "Yes, I will throw you back beyond the Dvina and beyond the Dnieper, and will rebuild against you that barrier which it was criminal and blind of Europe to allow to be destroyed. Yes, that is what will happen to you. That is what you have gained by alienating me!" And he walked silently several times up and down the room, his plump shoulders twitching.

He put his snuffbox into his waistcoat pocket, took it out again, raised it several times to his nose, and stopped in front of Balashev. He paused, looked ironically straight into Balashev's eyes, and said in a quiet voice:
"And yet what a splendid reign your master might have had!"

Balashev, feeling it his duty to reply, said that from the Russian side things did not look so bleak. Napoleon was silent, still looking at him derisively and clearly not listening. Balashev said that in Russia the best results were expected from the war. Napoleon nodded condescendingly, as if to say: "I know it's your duty to say that, but you don't believe it yourself. I have convinced you."

When Balashev had finished, Napoleon again took out his snuffbox, sniffed at it, and stamped his foot twice on the floor as a signal. The door opened, a gentleman-in-waiting, bowing respectfully, handed the Emperor his hat and gloves; another brought him a handkerchief. Napoleon, without looking at them, turned to Balashev:

"Assure the Emperor Alexander from me," said he, taking his hat, "that I am as devoted to him as before: I know him thoroughly and very highly esteem his noble qualities. I will detain you no longer, General; you shall receive my letter to the Emperor."
And Napoleon went quickly to the door. Everyone in the reception room rushed forward and hurried down the staircase.
